newsitem.title: DUBAI: Nurses' Saudi lawyers want murder case dismissed.
newsitem.headline: Nurses' Saudi lawyers want murder case dismissed.

text.p: The lawyers of two British nurses on trial for murder in Saudi Arabia said on Saturday they had submitted a legal paper to authorities outlining flaws in the case in order to have it dismissed.

The move came less than two weeks after the Islamic sharia court in the eastern Saudi city of Khobar adjourned for an unspecified period for deliberation. At the last court session on July 7, the family of murdered nurse Yvonne Gilford had insisted on the death sentence if the accused were found guilty.

Deborah Parry, 38, and Lucille McLauchlan, 31, are charged with murdering their 55-year-old colleague in December at a medical complex in nearby Dhahran. The women say they were forced into making confessions to the crime, which they later withdrew. Both say they are innocent.

"A comprehensive legal memorandum covering many aspects of the defence in the Gilford murder case was presented by the Law Firm of Salah al-Hejailan this week to the court...with copies to the top Saudi Arabian authorities as well as the minister of justice," the legal firm said in a statement.

"The memorandum evaluates the discredited confessions and other evidence which has been disclosed to date and also sets forth the basis for disqualifying the Gilford family from having any say in this ordeal under the worst scenario," it said.
In its most recent session, the court ruled Gilford's brother Frank had the right to demand execution if her alleged killers were found guilty as charged.

Islamic sharia law enforced in the kingdom gives the victim's heirs the right to decide for or against capital punishment if the court finds the accused guilty and says the death penalty is justified.

If Parry and McLauchlan are found guilty, they could face public beheading by the sword, the common form of execution in Saudi Arabia. Legal experts said it would be the first time Western women were executed in Saudi Arabia.
At least 68 people have been beheaded in the kingdom this year for crimes such as murder, armed robbery and drugs smuggling.
The statement from the law firm said it had arranged for the families of the two nurses to return to Saudi Arabia next weekend on the latest of several visits.
"This will hopefully be the last visit before the case is dismissed," the firm said.
